post_text:
I almost snatched the project back from him on a Tuesday morning.

He was three days behind schedule, staring at the whiteboard with quiet exhaustion.

My immediate reflex was to step in, rewrite the plan, and finish the delivery myself before midnight.

We often dress up our impatience as mentorship because playing the hero feeds our ego and quiets our own anxiety.

Instead, I swallowed the urge, stayed in my chair, and asked him what compromises he wanted to make.

He walked into the leadership meeting alone, took the heat for the delay, and renegotiated the timeline without flinching.

Over the next few days, he resolved every conflict and delivered an outcome far cleaner than the one I had mapped out in my own mind.

He did not need my answers; he needed the space to endure the discomfort of finding his own.

This is where teams usually get comfortable.

The hardest part of seniority is staying quiet long enough to let someone else discover their competence.
lesson_extracted: True mentorship requires suppressing your own ego and allowing others the discomfort necessary to build competence.
